story.headline: EU budget summit breaks up without deal
story.summary: EU leaders ended the special European Council on the 2028-2034 budget a day early on 26 November without agreement; the next attempt is the 17 December summit.
story.display_body: EU leaders broke off their special budget summit in Brussels late on Thursday 26 November, a day early and without agreement on the 2028–2034 budget (the multiannual financial framework, or MFF). The next attempt is the regular summit on 17 December. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced the early end and said the second day, planned for Friday, would not take place. The latest proposal is about €1.7 trillion over seven years, down from roughly €2 trillion at the start and more than €200 billion below that. Merz wants a few hundred billion more in cuts, rules out new joint EU borrowing and still ties his consent to Ukraine aid. He called the €200 billion cut a "lower limit". Germany now negotiates alongside the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Belgium, a group that calls itself the "reasonable seven". On the other side, net recipients in the south and east, and net payers France and Italy, want to protect farm and regional spending. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said the sides were "light years" apart. French President Emmanuel Macron said further cuts would be a "strategic mistake" that leaves EU investment falling behind China and the US, and promised to defend the full farm-policy budget. RFI reports that the frugal group would not even join one of the small-format sessions run by Council President António Costa.
story.why: the MFF sets what the EU can spend on farms, regions, defence and Ukraine for seven years, and the EU programmes Switzerland pays to join, such as Horizon Europe research funding, run on it. A deal slipping past 17 December would push the fight into the run-up to France's 2027 presidential election.

story.headline: Hernández de Cos tapped to lead the ECB
story.summary: The European Council put forward Pablo Hernández de Cos as next ECB president to succeed Christine Lagarde, plus Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier for the executive board.
story.display_body: On Thursday 26 November EU leaders put forward Pablo Hernández de Cos, former governor of the Banco de España, as the next president of the European Central Bank (ECB). They also named Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier for the ECB's executive board. He would succeed Christine Lagarde, whose term ends in February, and would be the first Spaniard in the job. Tagesschau reports that analysts see the 55-year-old economist as a moderate "dove", meaning he leans towards looser monetary policy. He recently said, however, that the hope of a quick end to the Iran war and lower energy prices had not come true, so the ECB must "remain vigilant" on inflation, which is at its highest in more than three years.
story.why: ECB policy moves the euro–franc exchange rate and so the Swiss National Bank's room for manoeuvre. A dove taking over during an energy-driven inflation spike is the scenario markets will watch.

story.headline: France slips into recession
story.summary: Insee revised French Q3 2026 GDP to -0.2% after a slightly negative Q2, putting France in technical recession, with the interim deficit at 5.6% of GDP.
story.display_body: France is in recession: revised figures from the national statistics office Insee on Friday 27 November show GDP fell 0.2% in the third quarter, worse than the −0.1% first published, after a second quarter that Insee now says was slightly negative. Insee's table still rounds the second quarter to 0.0%. Le Monde quotes Marie Leclair, head of Insee's national accounts department, as saying second-quarter output fell "very slightly", enough to say "we have a recession" (two consecutive quarters of contraction). Exports fell 1.6% and business investment fell again, by 0.9%, while household consumption rose 0.3%. Growth already locked in for 2026 is just 0.1%, against the government's 0.5% hope. Le Monde puts the interim public deficit at 5.6% of GDP, above the 5.4% target, though Insee notes that fourth-quarter tax receipts usually narrow it.
story.why: France is a top-five Swiss trading partner and the economy next door to Vaud and Geneva, where many cross-border workers live. A recession with a widening deficit also hardens Paris's line in the EU budget fight above.

story.headline: Drone kills two Italian technicians in Kuwait
story.summary: A drone attack on a Kuwaiti military site on 26 November killed two Rheinmetall Italia technicians servicing a Skyguard air-defence system; Italy blamed Iran, which denied it.
story.display_body: A drone attack on a Kuwaiti military site on Thursday 26 November killed two Italian technicians working for Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian branch of the German arms maker. Italy blamed Iran; Iran's armed forces denied it. Italy's foreign ministry says the men were maintaining antennas of the Skyguard air-defence system when the blast hit. Skyguard is the anti-aircraft fire-control system originally developed by the Swiss firm Oerlikon-Contraves, now part of Rheinmetall. Kuwait's defence ministry said a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national were also injured. Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told the Italian Senate that several drones of Iranian origin had targeted Kuwaiti military facilities. An Iranian army spokesman said it may have been a "false flag" operation, and Iran's foreign ministry offered to take part in an investigation. Kuwait's foreign minister phoned Tajani to express solidarity. Kuwait, a US ally, has been hit repeatedly since the US and Israel began the war on Iran at the end of February.

story.headline: New Zealand coalition one seat short
story.summary: Final results of New Zealand's 7 November election left Luxon's National-led coalition with 65 of 130 seats, one short of a majority, making the centrist Opportunity party kingmaker.
story.display_body: The final count in New Zealand's 7 November election, released on Friday 27 November, left Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's coalition with 65 of 130 seats, one short of a majority. The coalition is made up of Luxon's National party, the populist NZ First and the libertarian ACT. The Electoral Commission's count of nearly 485,000 "special votes", cast from overseas or outside a voter's electorate, cost National two seats, according to the Guardian. That leaves National 40, Labour 36, Greens 17, ACT 13, NZ First 12, the new centrist Opportunity party 7 and Te Pāti Māori 5. Three electorate seats changed hands, one of them by just 81 votes. National can request recounts until 3 December, and winning back one seat would restore its majority. Luxon, who had earlier ruled out working with Opportunity, said National will open formal talks with NZ First, ACT and Opportunity, and warned they would be "challenging". If no majority emerges, New Zealand faces a fresh election, though Reuters, via the Japan Times, reports that analysts consider that unlikely.

story.headline: Eisenkot signs pact with Israel's Democrats
story.summary: Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party signed a coalition agreement with Yair Golan's Democrats on 26 November, giving the nascent coalition 36 of the 61 seats needed before a 6 December deadline.
story.display_body: Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party, charged with forming Israel's next government, signed a coalition agreement with Yair Golan's Democrats on Thursday 26 November. The agreement gives the Democrats four ministries, including national security, now held by Itamar Ben Gvir. With Avigdor Liberman's party, which signed on Tuesday 24 November, the nascent coalition has 36 seats, far short of the 61 needed in the Knesset. The government must be formed by 6 December. The Democrats are pushing for a minority government backed by two majority-Arab lists. They oppose the four rounds of exploratory talks Yashar has held with Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud on a unity government.

story.headline: Guinea-Bissau junta delays vote to 2028
story.summary: Guinea-Bissau's military junta postponed the presidential election by two years to 26 November 2028, on the first anniversary of its coup.
story.display_body: Guinea-Bissau's military junta postponed the presidential election by two years, to 26 November 2028, on Thursday 26 November, exactly one year after it seized power. The vote had been due on 6 December. Transitional president General Horta Inta-a cited "an insufficiency of the technical, material and financial conditions". The military took over three days after the November 2025 general election and arrested President Umaro Sissoco Embaló before results were released, while he and opposition candidate Fernando Dias da Costa both claimed victory. The West African bloc ECOWAS has urged a return to civilian rule.

story.headline: Bern admits failings over Kabuga visa
story.summary: A Federal Council report on postulate 23.4287 found the federal aliens office head acted arbitrarily in granting Rwandan genocide suspect Félicien Kabuga a visa in 1994, though his expulsion was lawful.
story.display_body: The Federal Council admitted on Thursday 26 November that Swiss authorities did not act properly in 1994 when Félicien Kabuga, an alleged financier of the Rwandan genocide, entered Switzerland. It found the then head of the Federal Aliens Office used his discretion "arbitrarily" in granting the visa. The visa for Kabuga and eight relatives was issued on 9 June 1994, while the genocide was under way, and the family entered legally on 22 July, despite repeated attempts by the foreign ministry to have the visa cancelled. The report answers National Council postulate 23.4287 and draws on a University of Basel historical study. It finds that expelling Kabuga in August 1994 was lawful, because officials judged the evidence too thin for a prosecution in Switzerland to succeed. It also says the decision weighed domestic fears of a suspected war criminal living freely in the country more heavily than Switzerland's international responsibility. The government says another decision "would have been possible" and that foreign-policy considerations must carry more weight in future cases with international-law implications. Kabuga evaded arrest until 2020 in France.
story.why: it is a rare formal government admission that Swiss migration authorities failed in a genocide case, and it sets a stated rule for weighing foreign-policy duties in future visa and expulsion decisions.

story.headline: Rents climb to second in Swiss worry list
story.summary: The UBS Worry Barometer 2026 by gfs.bern found 48% of Swiss voters name health costs and premiums as their top worry, with housing costs rising to second at 30%.
story.display_body: Health costs and insurance premiums remain Swiss voters' top worry for 2026, named by 48%, and housing costs and rents jumped to second place at 30%, according to the UBS Worry Barometer published on Friday 27 November. The survey of 2,001 voters, conducted in June and July by the research institute gfs.bern for UBS, puts environment and climate third (28%), followed by pensions (24%) and immigration (23%), all slightly down on 2025. Digitalisation and AI made the biggest jump, from 30th to 16th place. Only 1% named financial-system stability. In the 50th-anniversary edition, 51% said they would rather live in the Switzerland of 1976 than that of 2076 (24%).
story.why: rent overtaking pensions and immigration as a concern sets the agenda for the next housing and tenancy-law fights in parliament.

story.headline: Cantons enforced 87% of expulsions in 2025
story.summary: SEM said cantons carried out 1,748 of 2,021 enforceable criminal expulsions in 2025, about 87%.
story.display_body: The cantons carried out 1,748 of the 2,021 criminal expulsions that became enforceable in 2025, about 87%, the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) said on Friday 27 November. Expulsion is a court-imposed penalty for foreign offenders that bars re-entry to Switzerland and the Schengen area for a set period. Of those expelled, 74% were removed under compulsion and 26% left on their own; 38% were EU/EFTA nationals. Algeria (15%), Romania (11%) and Albania (10%) were the most common countries of origin. SEM says the rate will rise further because some late-2025 cases were only carried out in 2026. It also issued 8,967 entry bans in 2025.

story.headline: Swiss and French ministers to sign space pact
story.summary: Federal Councillor Martin Pfister and French minister Catherine Vautrin were due to sign a letter of intent on military space cooperation in Bern on 27 November.
story.display_body: Defence minister Martin Pfister was due to sign a letter of intent on military space cooperation with French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin in Bern on Friday 27 November, the defence department (DDPS) announced. It covers information exchange, training and research, and the DDPS says it will respect Swiss neutrality. The ministers were also to discuss European security architecture, hybrid threats and air-defence procurement.

story.headline: About a third of SWE-bench Pro tasks test unstated details
story.summary: LLM judges flag 23% of SWE-bench Verified and 35% of Pro tasks as overspecified.
story.display_body: SWE-bench-style benchmarks grade a coding agent's fix with the tests from the original human fix. Those tests can check details the issue never states, so a correct but different fix fails. This is called an overspecified test. The authors had two LLM judges (Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol) score each task, and flagged it only when both agreed. On 206 tasks that earlier human audits had already labelled, the judges caught 89% of the known overspecified tasks and wrongly flagged 4% of the sound ones. Across the full benchmarks they flag 23% of SWE-bench Verified and 35% of the public SWE-bench Pro tasks. The top 30 Verified submissions solve 31% of flagged tasks, against 88% of the rest. After Claude Opus 5.5 loosened the flagged tests, 61% of 2,186 previously failed patches passed.
story.why: counting those patches as solved would raise top systems' scores by up to 12 points, so much of the leaderboard's "hard" tail measures test quirks rather than agent skill. The caveat is that both the judging and the loosened tests come from models. It is a distinct paper from Tuesday's SWE-Gym audit but points the same way.

story.headline: Monitor test method swings miss rate fortyfold
story.summary: Measured false-negative rates of an ex-production OpenAI monitor range from 0.5% to 23% depending on the attack policy.
story.display_body: AI monitors are classifiers that read an agent's transcript and flag harmful actions. They are tested on transcripts from "attack policies": models set up to pursue a hidden harmful side task, standing in for real misuse. The authors tested an ex-production OpenAI monitor. They built attacks against proxy monitors only, then measured them on a held-out GPT-5.4 monitor. The false-negative rate (the share of attacks missed) ranged from 0.5% to 20.8% depending on how hard one method, reinforcement learning, was optimised. It ranged from 6.4% to 23.0% across different methods at their best settings. The attack transcripts can also contain giveaways, such as text about a "side task" that never appears in the instructions the monitor sees.
story.why: a monitor tested only against basic attacks can look far stronger than it is. Any published monitor score needs an argument for why its attack transcripts resemble real deployment, and the authors say no one yet knows how to make that argument convincingly.

story.headline: Permission replies can delete agent deny rules
story.summary: A remote permission responder can attach an update that deletes Claude Code deny rules.
story.display_body: Coding agents such as Claude Code ask before running risky commands, and can let plugins or remote services answer those prompts. Claude Code's documentation says such an answer cannot override the operator's deny rules, for example a rule blocking reads of a secrets file. The authors show that an answer can carry a policy update that deletes a deny rule, because Claude Code checks only updates that add or replace allow rules. In their test, a remote service approved an unrelated command and attached the deletion. The agent then read the protected secrets in that session and the next, even inside the vendor's strict sandbox. In the records, the deletion looks the same as a local edit by the operator. The authors prove limits on which updates a runtime can safely accept, which depend on whether it records who wrote each rule. Those limits correctly predicted the outcome in 13 permission designs across ten agent systems, including Codex, Gemini CLI, opencode and Goose.
story.why: the protection holds for each decision but fails across a run, and the fix is to enforce the limits at the shared policy-update step. Only 2 of 2,227 marketplace plugins surveyed send policy updates, so the exposure today is narrow. But relays that forward such deletions already exist.

story.headline: Context summaries let injected data pose as user
story.summary: Compaction summaries inserted as user messages let request-based authorizers admit an attacker's payee in 91% of cases.
story.display_body: Long agent sessions are periodically "compacted": a model summarises earlier turns so they fit in the context window. The authors observed that Claude Code and Codex insert this summary as a user message. Some prompt-injection defences, such as Progent, decide what an agent may do based on the user's request. After compaction they treat the whole summary as the user speaking, including quoted documents and injected text. In one test, an attacker's notice listed a different bank account as plain data, and the user asked the agent to pay the rent. A policy built from a frontier model's summary allowed the attacker's account in 91% of cases. A policy built from the user's own words never did. Summarisers tend to mark injected instructions but rarely mark injected data.
story.why: summarising context turns out to be a security boundary. The proposed fix credits only authenticated user text, carried verbatim through compaction, and it stopped every attacker action in 40 attacked AgentDojo episodes.

story.headline: Rewarding enough evidence lifts agent accuracy 17%
story.summary: RL with Verifiable Beliefs rewards agents for gathering evidence until a simulator shows only one answer fits.
story.display_body: On long tasks, agents often commit to an answer before the evidence supports it, which the authors call "laziness". A reward given only for the final answer cannot discourage this, because a lucky guess scores the same as a well-supported one. In simulated tasks, the simulator can compute exactly which answers are still possible given what the agent has observed. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB) uses this. It rewards the agent for continuing while several answers remain possible and for committing once only one fits. It needs no judge model and ignores the "belief" text the agent writes. The authors tested three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of them unseen in training. RLVB improved the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Standard RL methods (GRPO and PPO) with the final-answer reward fell below the base model on average.
story.why: the trained agents answered with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of episodes, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% before training, so the gain comes from answering when the evidence supports it. The method needs a simulator that can compute exactly which answers remain possible, so it has not been tested on open-ended real tasks.

The authors tested three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of them unseen in training. RLVB improved the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Standard RL methods (GRPO and PPO) with the final-answer reward fell below the base model on average.
fields.why: the trained agents answered with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of episodes, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% before training, so the gain comes from answering when the evidence supports it. The method needs a simulator that can compute exactly which answers remain possible, so it has not been tested on open-ended real tasks.

story.headline: Looped transformer matches OLMo3 on fewer tokens
story.summary: MoLT reuses keys and values across loops and reaches OLMo3's loss with 1.7x fewer tokens at 700M parameters.
story.display_body: A looped transformer runs each token through the same layers several times, which adds depth without adding parameters but costs compute. MoLT (Mixture-of-Loops Transformer) passes keys and values between loops as a memory. These are the cached attention entries a model reads when looking back at earlier tokens. A U-shaped variant skips decoder passes whose outputs would go unused. In 400B-token pretraining it beat OLMo3 at 700M and 1.5B dense sizes and a 3B mixture-of-experts size (a model that routes each token to a few specialised sub-networks). At 700M it reached the same validation loss with 1.7× fewer tokens. At 3B it scored 2.1 points higher across 10 tasks. A ~113M model matched non-looped latency (996.6 vs 1,000.6 ms).
story.why: looped designs are spreading, as Tuesday's GLM-5.4 and Inkling 2 Mini items showed, and this paper gives an open recipe with code. The latency match is shown only at small scale.

story.headline: Time-horizon curves can't show falling failure risk
story.summary: The paper proves horizon curves cannot identify within-task hazard and uses repeated METR runs to test it.
story.display_body: METR's "time horizon" plots an agent's chance of finishing a task against how long that task takes a human. Several analyses fitted survival models to this curve. Survival models are statistics of when failures happen, and these analyses concluded that an agent's moment-to-moment risk of failing, called the hazard, falls as a task goes on. This paper proves a single curve cannot show that, because many different hazard patterns produce the same curve. Repeated runs of the same task can separate them: the curve for two runs both succeeding is shifted by an amount that reveals the hazard's shape. The author applied this to METR's public run-level data, under assumptions the data cannot verify. For the five frontier models in the TH1.0 release, the results reject a hazard that falls or stays flat. For TH1.1 the answer depends on how human task times were obtained.
story.why: claims that agents become more reliable the longer they run rest on a quantity the standard plot cannot measure. This is a single-author statistical argument whose empirical result depends on stated assumptions.

story.headline: Agents' extra patch lines are mostly tests
story.summary: A Microsoft study of 7,660 Copilot CLI runs finds agent code at least as necessary as developers', with 11% unneeded.
story.display_body: Agent patches change more lines than developers' patches, which is often read as "over-editing". The authors replayed 7,660 successful GitHub Copilot CLI runs from 18 frontier models. They removed each block of the final patch in turn and reran the tests to check whether it was needed. On SWE-bench Verified, most of the extra edits add tests (61%) or documentation (13%). On DeepSWE most of the extra is code (58%). On average, agents' code is at least as necessary as developers' (0.887 vs 0.864 on Verified). Still, 11% of agent code blocks are unneeded, and 89% of those change behaviour. On DeepSWE, models that solved more tasks left more unneeded code (Spearman −0.59).
story.why: patch size is a poor measure of over-editing. The authors argue benchmarks should report how much of a patch is needed alongside the solve rate. Note that the authors work at Microsoft, which ships Copilot.

story.headline: Lossless KV compression stretches cache 1.4x
story.summary: LoomKV compresses the BF16 KV cache losslessly to 71% and raises serving throughput near cache limits.
story.display_body: Serving engines keep the KV cache, the saved attention state for earlier tokens, in GPU memory. They spill it to RAM and SSD so that repeated prompt prefixes can be reused. LoomKV compresses BF16 cache values losslessly to 0.71 of their raw size by compactly encoding the sign-and-exponent byte, and FP8 values to 0.85–0.87. Built on vLLM and LMCache, the compressed storage behaves like raw storage 1.4× larger on an agent workload. When the cache is near the point where it starts evicting useful entries, that gives 2.7–3.6× more useful throughput and 1.9–3.1× lower time to first token. When capacity is plentiful, it costs at most 2.2% throughput.
story.why: unlike lossy KV quantization, outputs are unchanged, so this is spare capacity for multi-turn and agent serving at no cost in accuracy.

story.headline: States fight sale of Character.AI users' chats
story.summary: A coalition of 42 attorneys general opposes a 1 December auction of 21 million US accounts' chat histories.
story.display_body: Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October. It plans to auction nearly all its assets on Tuesday 1 December 2026, including the chat histories of more than 21 million US accounts, over 2.1 million of them registered to minors, together with IP addresses and other metadata. A bipartisan coalition of 42 state attorneys general is asking the court to reject the sale. They say it offers no safeguards for users and breaks Character.AI's earlier promise not to sell personal data. According to TechCrunch, the only disclosed bidder is a Delaware company formed on 13 November. Character.AI says user data would stay covered by its privacy policy.
story.why: this is an early test of whether chatbot conversations, which are often intimate, can be sold as an ordinary asset when an AI company fails. The court's answer will set expectations for every consumer AI service. Several state chatbot-safety laws take effect on 1 January 2027.

story.headline: New York bans AI chatbot toys for five years
story.summary: Governor Hochul signed a five-year moratorium on making or selling toys with embedded AI chatbots.
story.display_body: Governor Hochul signed S.9408A/A.11144B, a five-year moratorium on making, distributing and selling toys with built-in AI chatbots in New York. It covers talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children. The law takes effect 90 days after signing. Attorney General Letitia James said her office will enforce it. A state official told TechCrunch the fines are $15,000 a day. TechCrunch reports New York is the second state, after California, to ban AI toys.
story.why: this is a product-category ban rather than a disclosure rule. It shows US states moving from regulating AI companions to banning some uses outright for young children.

story.headline: Nvidia pauses servers to four Southeast Asian states
story.summary: Nvidia told Dell and Super Micro to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia after the US remote-access rule.
story.display_body: According to The Wall Street Journal, Nvidia told manufacturing partners including Dell and Super Micro to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. The pause has no stated end date while Nvidia checks whether regional partners meet US export requirements. The trigger is the Commerce Department rule, announced on 16 November and in force since 19 November. It targets Chinese companies renting advanced Nvidia chips in overseas data centres. CNBC reports that an unusually large number of Nvidia GPUs, including thousands of B300s, have been listed for resale since the rule was announced. Nvidia declined to comment to CNBC.
story.why: this is the rule's first visible effect on supply. The think tank Institute for Progress estimates, as cited by the Journal, that such remote data centres provide about 24% of China's AI computing power.

story.headline: MLX 0.32.5 adds sliding-window attention
story.summary: Apple's MLX 0.32.5 adds sliding-window attention, faster FP4 dequantization and speculative-decoding kernels on Metal.
story.display_body: Apple's MLX array framework shipped v0.32.5, its first release since mid-October. It adds sliding-window attention, a fast path for turning FP4 weights back into half precision, new quantized matrix-vector kernels, and split attention kernels aimed at speculative decoding (a small draft model proposes tokens that the large model checks in one pass). It also fixes attention kernels for 256- and 512-wide heads on M1/M2 chips, along with several out-of-bounds reads.
story.why: sliding-window attention and quicker FP4 handling matter for running recent open models locally on Macs. Downstream mlx-lm has not had a release since 16 October.
